definition: Eager to please others and quick to go along with what they want.
example: The complaisant host rearranged the seating chart twice to suit his guests' preferences.
nuance: Complaisant means eager to please others; the look-alike complacent means smugly satisfied with yourself.
prompt: A college student's roommate asks her to change the hours when she practices the cello.
options: Always complaisant, Mara agreed to shift her practice hours so her roommate could sleep.
Mara grew complaisant about her habits and assumed nothing she did needed improving.
Being so complaisant, Mara flatly refused to move even one minute of her weekly routine for anyone.
The complaisant cello sat in its case in the corner of the dorm room.
reasons: Readily giving in to someone else's request is exactly what a complaisant person does.
Smug self-satisfaction describes complacent, a look-alike word, not eagerness to please.
Stubborn refusal is the reverse of obligingly going along with others.
An object cannot try to please anyone, so the word has nothing to describe here.

practice.prompt: A tour guide leads a large group through an old city neighborhood.
options: The complaisant map showed the route in tiny print that nobody could read.
The complaisant guide added a stop at a bakery when several travelers asked for one.
The complaisant guide ignored every question and kept walking at his own brisk pace.
Having led the tour for years, the guide felt complaisant and never bothered to update his facts.
reasons: A map has no wish to please, so calling it complaisant makes no sense.
Changing the plan to satisfy the group's wishes shows a readiness to oblige.
Brushing off the group's needs is the opposite of trying to accommodate them.
Lazy contentment with past work is complacency, which is easily confused with this word.
